overview: Mandan communities built farming villages along the Missouri River and became important partners in Plains exchange. The imported outline lies near their historic village country in present-day North Dakota, but its dates describe map coverage. Mandan people remain a distinct people within today’s Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.

periods.title: Earthlodge villages along the Missouri
periods.summary: Double Ditch was occupied approximately from 1490 to 1785, within a longer regional village history.

periods.title: Relocation and river trade
periods.summary: Communities relocated, and the Fort Clark trading post connected a Mandan village to steamboat commerce.

periods.title: Survival and new communities
periods.summary: Epidemic survivors joined neighbors farther north while maintaining Mandan identity.

periods.title: Displacement and continuing nationhood
periods.summary: Dam construction disrupted river-bottom communities; Mandan people continue within the MHA Nation.

items.text: Double Ditch, north of present-day Bismarck, preserves a Mandan village occupied for roughly three centuries, from around 1490 to 1785. Its name is misleadingly modest: researchers have identified four successive defensive ditches. The settlement’s changing boundaries record a community repeatedly rebuilding its surroundings.

Geophysical instruments revealed buried hearths, storage pits and two previously unrecognized fortifications at Double Ditch. Archaeologists then checked the signals through excavation. The combination uncovered parts of village life that a walk across the grassy surface could easily miss.

Mandan farmers raised corn, beans, squash, sunflowers and tobacco. Stored harvests supported village life and exchange with other Plains communities, while hunting supplied bison and other animals. A farming village could therefore be a trading destination as well as a place to grow dinner.

Community-authored teaching materials describe women owning and building earthlodges, with men helping move heavy logs. Wood, branches, grass and earth formed substantial homes. Mandan builders used clay in their coverings, and strong roofs could become places to sit and watch village activity.

Relatives often placed their lodges near one another. Children could play close to family while adults visited and worked. The same teaching account describes cottonwood collected after spring ice had knocked trees down, then left to dry: housebuilding began well before the house appeared.

Harvest preservation required practical defenses against hungry animals. Raised drying platforms helped keep food away from dogs. Women dried crops for later use, turning a short growing season into meals that could last through much colder weather.

Underground food caches were lined with grasses and sticks, reached by a ladder and carefully covered. Some were inside lodges, others outside. Concealing the lid protected an important family store: the pantry could be beneath your feet.

In the game called tchung-kee, Mandan and Hidatsa players rolled a small stone ring and threw long poles, trying to send a pole through the moving opening. The challenge joined timing, aim and competition. A little ring could demand a surprisingly large amount of skill.

The American Fur Company built Fort Clark beside a Mandan village in 1830 to 1831. In 1832, the steamboat Yellow Stone delivered goods and carried beaver pelts and bison robes back toward St. Louis. Village trade now connected households to a much longer commercial river route.

In 1837, the steamboat St. Peters arrived carrying people infected with smallpox. A devastating epidemic swept through the Mandan village at Fort Clark. Survivors left to join Hidatsa communities near the Knife River. These were catastrophic human losses, followed by survival and rebuilding rather than the end of Mandan people.

Commissioned in 1905, Sitting Rabbit’s remarkable map stretched along a canvas more than 23 feet long. It recorded Missouri River places and older villages through Mandan knowledge and pictorial detail. The river’s bends were adapted to the long format, creating a historical landscape that could be unrolled.

The Garrison Dam project displaced families from fertile Missouri bottomlands in the twentieth century. MHA Nation’s history describes lost farms and communities and relocation onto less productive uplands. A change in the river’s level could therefore alter food production, neighboring relationships and the places where family memories lived.

A modern Mandan writing sample is “Ráátinitak shí’sh.” The MHA Nation website translates it as “It is good that you all arrived”. The site prints distinct Hidatsa and Arikara welcomes beside it, making clear that the three affiliated peoples have different languages.
A Mandan alphabet coloring book published in 2016 invites children to trace letters and words and use a color key. Its exercises make literacy something a child can practice with a pencil.

MHA Nation’s language programs maintain separate work for Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara. Mentor-and-apprentice learning connects experienced speakers with learners who can become future teachers. Modern classes and children’s resources belong to the continuing history of these communities.

ending.text: The imported endpoint of 1783 is not an ending for the Mandan people. Epidemics, relocation and later flooding of river-bottom lands transformed community life. Mandan identity and language work continue within the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara Nation.
